checkpoints: Redis's GEOADD command follows the mathematical (x, y) axis convention, expecting arguments in the order key, longitude, latitude, member — latitude comes second, not first.

Swapping latitude and longitude still produces a syntactically and semantically valid pair of numbers for GEOADD, so Redis accepts and stores the coordinate without any validation error; it just encodes a location on the opposite side of the (lng, lat) convention, for example landing Ho Chi Minh City's (10.76, 106.66) somewhere off the coast of West Africa.

An always-empty nearby-driver result combined with drivers actively pinging and zero thrown exceptions is a signature that data was written to the wrong place, not that the query logic itself is broken — this points investigation toward the write path (GEOADD) rather than the read path (GEOSEARCH).

Both the write (GEOADD) and the read (GEOSEARCH with FROMLONLAT/BYRADIUS) execute successfully as syntactically valid Redis commands even with the coordinates swapped, which is exactly why this class of bug throws no exception anywhere and can ship unnoticed — only the underlying data is wrong, not the code path.

A one-line reorder of the arguments fixes the immediate symptom, but the durable fix is structural: funnel every position write through a single method that takes an explicitly named `{ lat, lng }` parameter and performs the swap into `(lng, lat)` internally in exactly one place, so no caller can pass raw positional coordinates directly into a GEO write.

A proving regression test writes a driver at a known coordinate, then runs the nearby search with a very small radius (e.g. 10m) around that exact point and asserts the driver comes back at roughly zero distance — this test fails against the swapped-argument version and passes once the order is corrected.

Because GEO writes and reads are two separate operations with no cross-validation, an argument-order bug in the write path is invisible to any error handling on the read path, making it a class of bug that silently corrupts data while every individual operation reports success.
